cards.q: Which structure secretes gonadotropin releasing hormone?
cards.a: The hypothalamus.
options: The gonads themselves
The hypothalamus
The anterior pituitary
The posterior pituitary
cards.explanation: GnRH is made by a small population of hypothalamic neurons whose axons end at the median eminence. The anterior pituitary is the target of GnRH, not its source, and it responds by releasing LH and FSH. The posterior pituitary stores oxytocin and ADH made in the hypothalamus, but GnRH is not among them. The gonads sit at the bottom of the axis and send hormones back up, so they are the end of the chain rather than the start.

cards.q: By what route does gonadotropin releasing hormone reach the anterior pituitary?
cards.a: Through the hypothalamic hypophyseal portal veins.
options: Through the general arterial circulation
By axonal transport down the infundibulum to the gland
By diffusion across the sella turcica
Through the hypothalamic hypophyseal portal veins
cards.explanation: The portal veins carry GnRH from the median eminence directly to the gonadotropes, so a tiny amount of hormone reaches a high local concentration. If GnRH had to travel through the general circulation it would be diluted and degraded long before arriving. Axonal transport down the infundibulum is how oxytocin and ADH reach the posterior pituitary, which is a different lobe with a different delivery system. Simple diffusion across bone is not a transport route the body uses.

cards.q: Which two hormones does the anterior pituitary release in response to gonadotropin releasing hormone?
cards.a: Luteinizing hormone and follicle stimulating hormone.
options: Luteinizing hormone and follicle stimulating hormone
Adrenocorticotropic hormone and thyroid stimulating hormone
Oxytocin and prolactin
Inhibin and activin
cards.explanation: One releasing hormone drives both gonadotropins, which is why LH and FSH tend to move together when the hypothalamus changes its output. ACTH and TSH are also anterior pituitary hormones but they answer to CRH and TRH and run the adrenal and thyroid axes. Oxytocin comes from the posterior pituitary, and prolactin is anterior pituitary but is controlled mainly by dopamine inhibition rather than GnRH. Inhibin and activin are gonadal peptides that feed back on the pituitary rather than being released by it.

cards.q: In what pattern is gonadotropin releasing hormone normally released?
cards.a: In pulses, roughly every one to three hours.
options: As a single large bolus once each morning
Only in the hours surrounding ovulation
In pulses, roughly every one to three hours
At a continuous steady level all day
cards.explanation: The gonadotrope requires a pulsatile signal, and the frequency of those pulses is itself information that shifts the LH to FSH ratio. A continuous steady level does the opposite of what students expect: it downregulates the GnRH receptor and shuts the axis off. A single daily bolus describes the pattern of some other rhythms, such as the cortisol morning peak, not GnRH. Release only around ovulation would leave the axis silent for most of the cycle, and the follicular phase depends on ongoing gonadotropin support.

cards.q: To which chemical class do luteinizing hormone and follicle stimulating hormone belong?
cards.a: Glycoproteins.
options: Catecholamines
Eicosanoids
Glycoproteins
Steroids
cards.explanation: LH and FSH are glycoprotein hormones built from a shared alpha subunit and a distinct beta subunit, so they act at surface receptors and cannot cross the plasma membrane. Steroids describe the gonadal hormones further down the axis, estrogen, progesterone and testosterone, which do enter cells and act on nuclear receptors. Catecholamines such as epinephrine are tyrosine derivatives from the adrenal medulla. Eicosanoids such as prostaglandins are made from arachidonic acid and act locally rather than as pituitary messengers.

cards.q: Which gonadal hormone selectively suppresses follicle stimulating hormone without much effect on luteinizing hormone?
cards.a: Inhibin.
options: Inhibin
Testosterone
Progesterone
Activin
cards.explanation: Inhibin is the peptide that lets the gonad report gamete production separately from steroid production, and it acts on the gonadotrope to turn FSH down specifically. Testosterone and progesterone are steroids that suppress both gonadotropins, largely by slowing GnRH pulses at the hypothalamus. Activin is the counterpart of inhibin and pushes FSH up rather than down. This selectivity is why a person with damaged gamete producing tissue can show a high FSH while LH stays close to normal.

cards.q: From which precursor molecule are the gonadal steroid hormones synthesized?
cards.a: Cholesterol.
options: Tyrosine
Tryptophan
Arachidonic acid
Cholesterol
cards.explanation: Every steroid hormone, gonadal and adrenal alike, is built by modifying the cholesterol ring system, which is why the synthetic pathways for these hormones overlap so heavily. Tyrosine is the precursor for thyroid hormone and the catecholamines. Tryptophan gives rise to serotonin and then melatonin. Arachidonic acid is the starting point for prostaglandins and other eicosanoids, which matter in labor but are not steroids.

cards.q: In males, and during most of the female cycle, what type of feedback do the gonadal steroids exert on the hypothalamus and pituitary?
cards.a: Negative feedback.
options: No feedback at all
Negative feedback
Positive feedback
Feedforward control
cards.explanation: The default arrangement is negative feedback, so rising testosterone or estrogen slows GnRH pulses and reduces LH and FSH, keeping the axis stable. Positive feedback is the exception, appearing only when estrogen from the dominant follicle stays high for a day or more just before ovulation. Feedforward describes anticipating a disturbance before it happens, which is not how the gonadal steroids act here. An axis with no feedback would have no way to hold hormone levels in range.

cards.q: A patient is given a gonadotropin releasing hormone agonist as a continuous infusion for several weeks. What happens to luteinizing hormone and follicle stimulating hormone?
cards.a: Both fall well below baseline.
options: Both remain at their baseline levels
Both fall well below baseline
Both rise and stay elevated
LH rises while FSH falls
cards.explanation: After a brief initial flare, continuous exposure downregulates and desensitizes the GnRH receptor on the gonadotrope, so LH and FSH fall and the gonads go quiet. Sustained elevation would be the answer if the receptor did not desensitize, but pulsatility is exactly what the gonadotrope requires. A split response with LH up and FSH down would need something acting selectively, such as inhibin. Unchanged levels would mean the receptor ignored a continuous agonist, which is not what happens.

cards.q: Both gonads are surgically removed from an adult. Predict what happens to luteinizing hormone and follicle stimulating hormone.
cards.a: Both rise, because negative feedback is lost.
options: Both fall, because there is no target organ
Both stay the same, because the pituitary is intact
LH falls while FSH rises
Both rise, because negative feedback is lost
cards.explanation: Gonadal steroids and inhibin are the brake on the axis, so removing the gonads releases that brake and gonadotropins climb to high levels. Falling gonadotropins would require damage above the gonad, not below it, since the pituitary does not need a target to secrete. Unchanged levels would mean the axis has no feedback, which contradicts the whole design. A split response would require something suppressing LH selectively, and nothing here does that.

cards.q: A tumor secretes large amounts of inhibin into the circulation. Which pituitary hormone falls the most?
cards.a: Follicle stimulating hormone.
options: Follicle stimulating hormone
Luteinizing hormone
Thyroid stimulating hormone
Adrenocorticotropic hormone
cards.explanation: Inhibin acts on the gonadotrope to suppress FSH specifically, so FSH drops while LH is only modestly affected. LH answers mainly to GnRH pulse frequency and to steroid feedback, so it does not track inhibin closely. TSH and ACTH belong to separate axes with their own releasing hormones and their own feedback signals, and inhibin does not reach into them. This selective suppression is the reason FSH is the better clinical marker of gamete producing tissue.

cards.q: The pituitary stalk is severed, cutting the hypothalamic hypophyseal portal vessels. Predict the effect on luteinizing hormone and follicle stimulating hormone.
cards.a: Both fall, because GnRH can no longer reach the gonadotropes.
options: Both are unchanged, because the pituitary is autonomous
LH falls while FSH climbs sharply
Both fall, because GnRH can no longer reach the gonadotropes
Both rise, because inhibitory input is removed
cards.explanation: The portal vessels are the only practical delivery route for GnRH, so cutting them starves the gonadotropes of their releasing signal and both gonadotropins fall. Gonadotropins are driven by a releasing hormone rather than held down by an inhibiting one, so removing hypothalamic input lowers them. Prolactin is the hormone that rises after stalk section, because dopamine is the inhibiting signal it loses. The pituitary is not autonomous for LH and FSH, and nothing in this lesion selectively suppresses one gonadotropin.

cards.q: Estradiol from a dominant follicle stays above its threshold concentration for about two days. Predict the effect on luteinizing hormone.
cards.a: LH rises steeply into a surge.
options: LH stays flat until progesterone rises
LH oscillates around its previous mean
LH rises steeply into a surge
LH falls further, deepening the suppression
cards.explanation: Sustained high estradiol flips the hypothalamic and pituitary response from negative to positive feedback, and the result is the LH surge that triggers ovulation about a day later. Continued suppression is what happens at low or briefly elevated estradiol, which is the pattern for most of the follicular phase. Progesterone rises after ovulation as a consequence of the surge, so waiting for it reverses the order of events. Simple oscillation would mean estradiol carried no information about follicle maturity.

cards.q: A man takes exogenous testosterone. Predict what happens to his own luteinizing hormone secretion.
cards.a: It falls, because testosterone feeds back negatively.
options: It falls, because testosterone feeds back negatively
It rises, to match the higher androgen level
It is unchanged, because the source is external
It rises first and then oscillates
cards.explanation: The hypothalamus and pituitary read total circulating androgen and cannot tell an injected molecule from one made by the Leydig cells, so LH is suppressed. Rising LH would require positive feedback from androgen, which does not exist in the male axis. The axis has no way to identify the source of a steroid, so calling it external does not exempt it from feedback. Sustained oscillation is not the pattern, because the suppression here is steady rather than intermittent.

cards.q: Laboratory results show low luteinizing hormone, low follicle stimulating hormone, and low gonadal steroids. Where does the problem lie?
cards.a: In the hypothalamus or pituitary.
options: In the gonads themselves
In the adrenal cortex
In the posterior pituitary instead
In the hypothalamus or pituitary
cards.explanation: When the gonad fails, its steroids fall but the gonadotropins climb because negative feedback is lost, so low steroids with low gonadotropins points upstream to the hypothalamus or pituitary. Gonadal failure gives the opposite gonadotropin pattern and is the distinction worth memorizing. The adrenal cortex contributes androgens but is not the driver of LH and FSH. The posterior pituitary releases oxytocin and ADH and has no role in the gonadal axis.

cards.q: A teenager has never entered puberty. Testing shows undetectable gonadotropin releasing hormone pulses, low luteinizing hormone, and low estradiol. Trace the axis and predict what happens if pulsatile gonadotropin releasing hormone is delivered by pump.
cards.a: LH and FSH rise, then the ovary produces estradiol and follicles develop.
options: FSH rises but LH remains suppressed because it needs steroid priming
LH and FSH rise, then the ovary produces estradiol and follicles develop
LH and FSH stay low, because the pituitary has already atrophied permanently
Estradiol rises first and only later drives LH upward
cards.explanation: The lesion is at the top of the axis, so supplying the missing signal in its natural pulsatile pattern restarts everything below it: gonadotropes respond, gonadotropins rise, and the ovary makes estradiol and grows follicles. The pituitary in this situation is understimulated rather than destroyed, so it recovers once the signal arrives. Estradiol cannot come first, because the ovary needs gonadotropin support to make it. Both gonadotropins respond to GnRH, so a selective FSH only rise does not fit.

cards.q: The same gonadotropin releasing hormone agonist can be used either to start puberty or to shut the axis down. What determines which effect occurs?
cards.a: Whether it is delivered in pulses or continuously.
options: Whether it is given before or after breakfast
Whether it is delivered in pulses or continuously
Whether the dose is high or low
Whether the patient is male or female
cards.explanation: The gonadotrope reads the pattern of the signal, not just its presence: pulsatile delivery keeps receptors responsive and stimulates the axis, while continuous delivery downregulates them and suppresses it. Dose matters at the margins but cannot convert continuous exposure into a stimulating signal. The pattern rule holds in both sexes, since the same receptor is on the same cell type. Timing relative to meals has no bearing on GnRH receptor regulation.

cards.q: A woman takes a combined oral contraceptive containing estrogen and progestin. Trace the axis and explain why she does not ovulate.
cards.a: Steady steroid levels suppress gonadotropins, so no LH surge forms.
options: The pill blocks LH receptors on the follicle so the surge cannot act
The pill destroys the corpus luteum before ovulation can happen
The pill raises FSH so many follicles mature and none becomes dominant
Steady steroid levels suppress gonadotropins, so no LH surge forms
cards.explanation: Constant exogenous steroid holds the hypothalamus and pituitary under steady negative feedback, so gonadotropins stay low, no follicle reaches the estradiol output needed for positive feedback, and the LH surge never forms. Blocking LH receptors on the follicle is not how these steroids work, and it would not explain the low gonadotropins. The corpus luteum forms after ovulation, so it cannot be the thing preventing ovulation. FSH falls rather than rises, which is why multiple follicle recruitment is not the mechanism.

cards.q: A man using high dose anabolic androgens has a high serum testosterone but a very low sperm count. Which sequence explains the low sperm count?
cards.a: Suppressed LH lowers intratesticular testosterone despite the high serum level.
options: Suppressed LH lowers intratesticular testosterone despite the high serum level
The androgen directly poisons the developing sperm cells in the tubule
High serum testosterone raises FSH and exhausts the Sertoli cells
The androgen disrupts the blood testis barrier so that sperm leak into the blood
cards.explanation: Spermatogenesis depends on a testosterone concentration inside the seminiferous tubule far above the level in blood, and that local concentration comes from Leydig cells driven by LH. Exogenous androgen suppresses LH, the Leydig cells go quiet, and intratesticular testosterone collapses despite a high serum value. Direct toxicity to germ cells is not the mechanism, and it would not explain why the effect reverses when the drug stops. FSH falls rather than rises under this feedback, and barrier leakage is not what these drugs do.

cards.q: Which testicular cell carries luteinizing hormone receptors and secretes testosterone?
cards.a: The Leydig cell.
options: The spermatogonium
The myoid cell
The Leydig cell
The Sertoli cell
cards.explanation: Leydig cells sit in the interstitial space between the tubules, respond to LH, and are the source of testosterone. Sertoli cells lie inside the tubule and carry FSH receptors instead, supporting the germ cells rather than making the main androgen. Spermatogonia are the dividing germ cells themselves and are the target of the hormonal support, not its source. Myoid cells are contractile cells around the tubule that help move sperm along and are not steroidogenic.

cards.q: Which testicular cell carries follicle stimulating hormone receptors and nurses the developing sperm?
cards.a: The Sertoli cell.
options: The spermatid
The epididymal cell
The Sertoli cell
The Leydig cell
cards.explanation: Sertoli cells line the seminiferous tubule, bind FSH, and provide the physical support and nutrients that germ cells need as they mature. Leydig cells respond to LH and make testosterone from the interstitium outside the tubule. A spermatid is a stage of the germ cell being supported, so it is the recipient rather than the nurse. Epididymal cells handle sperm maturation and storage after the sperm have already left the tubule.

cards.q: Which hormone do Sertoli cells secrete to feed back on follicle stimulating hormone?
cards.a: Inhibin.
options: Inhibin
Testosterone
Relaxin
Oxytocin
cards.explanation: Inhibin from the Sertoli cell is the feedback signal that tells the pituitary how well the tubule is working, and it selectively lowers FSH. Testosterone comes from the Leydig cell and suppresses both gonadotropins mainly by slowing GnRH pulses. Relaxin is a hormone of pregnancy, from the corpus luteum and placenta, with no role in this loop. Oxytocin is a posterior pituitary hormone acting on uterus and breast, not a Sertoli product.

cards.q: What is the function of androgen binding protein secreted by Sertoli cells?
cards.a: It keeps testosterone concentrated inside the seminiferous tubule.
options: It carries testosterone through the bloodstream to distant tissues
It converts testosterone into dihydrotestosterone
It blocks testosterone from reaching the germ cells
It keeps testosterone concentrated inside the seminiferous tubule
cards.explanation: Androgen binding protein holds testosterone in the tubular fluid at a concentration many times higher than in blood, which is the level germ cells require. Transport through the blood is handled by sex hormone binding globulin and albumin, which are different proteins with a different job. Conversion to dihydrotestosterone is done by the enzyme 5 alpha reductase, not by a binding protein. Blocking access would defeat the purpose, since germ cell development depends on high local androgen.

cards.q: What forms the blood testis barrier?
cards.a: Tight junctions between adjacent Sertoli cells.
options: The capillary endothelium of the testicular artery
Tight junctions between adjacent Sertoli cells
Tight junctions between Leydig cells
A basement membrane around each spermatogonium
cards.explanation: Sertoli cells are joined to each other by tight junctions that split the tubule into a basal compartment and an adluminal compartment, isolating the developing sperm. Leydig cells sit in the interstitium and are not joined into a barrier. A basement membrane surrounds the whole tubule rather than each germ cell, and it does not create the compartment split. The capillary endothelium is leaky enough in the interstitium that it cannot be the barrier that hides sperm antigens.

cards.q: Why does the immune system need to be kept away from developing sperm?
cards.a: Sperm appear after immune tolerance is set, so they read as foreign.
options: Sperm cannot survive contact with plasma proteins of any kind at all
Sperm appear after immune tolerance is set, so they read as foreign
Sperm carry bacterial antigens picked up from the epididymal duct
Sperm release histamine that would trigger inflammation
cards.explanation: Spermatogenesis begins at puberty, long after the immune system learned which antigens are self, so the haploid germ cells would be attacked as foreign without the barrier. Sperm do not acquire bacterial antigens in a healthy tract, so infection is not the explanation. Sperm are not a source of histamine, which comes from mast cells and basophils. Sperm do encounter proteins in seminal fluid and in the female tract, so blanket intolerance of plasma proteins is not the issue.

cards.q: Which enzyme converts testosterone to dihydrotestosterone?
cards.a: 5 alpha reductase.
options: Aromatase
17 beta hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase
Cholesterol desmolase
5 alpha reductase
cards.explanation: 5 alpha reductase makes dihydrotestosterone, the more potent androgen responsible for prostate growth and much of male external genital development. Aromatase does something different, converting androgens into estrogens, and it operates in fat, brain, and Sertoli cells. 17 beta hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase works earlier in the pathway, making testosterone from androstenedione. Cholesterol desmolase performs the first committed step of all steroid synthesis and is not specific to androgens.

cards.q: About how long does one full cycle of spermatogenesis take in humans?
cards.a: About 70 days.
options: About 70 days
About 7 days
About 14 days
About 6 months
cards.explanation: A spermatogonium takes roughly 64 to 74 days to become a mature spermatozoon, which is why treatments affecting sperm production take more than two months to show up in a semen analysis. Seven days is far too short for meiosis plus the whole remodeling of spermiogenesis. Fourteen days is the length of the luteal phase in the female cycle, a value students often import here by mistake. Six months overshoots and would make the process slower than any measured value.

cards.q: Sertoli cell function is selectively impaired so that these cells no longer respond to follicle stimulating hormone. Predict what happens to circulating inhibin and follicle stimulating hormone.
cards.a: Inhibin falls and FSH rises.
options: Both inhibin and FSH fall
Both inhibin and FSH rise
Inhibin falls and FSH rises
Inhibin rises and FSH falls
cards.explanation: Inhibin is a Sertoli product, so losing Sertoli responsiveness lowers inhibin, and with the brake off FSH climbs. A rise in inhibin with a fall in FSH describes the healthy tubule doing its job, the opposite of this lesion. Both falling would require damage to the pituitary as well as the tubule. Both rising is impossible here, because inhibin cannot rise from a cell that is not responding.

cards.q: A man has failure of the Leydig cells but intact pituitary function. Predict his luteinizing hormone and testosterone levels.
cards.a: High LH with low testosterone.
options: High LH with high testosterone
Low LH with high testosterone
High LH with low testosterone
Low LH with low testosterone
cards.explanation: The Leydig cell is the source of testosterone, so testosterone falls, and the lost negative feedback lets LH climb. Low LH with low testosterone would point to a hypothalamic or pituitary problem rather than a gonadal one, which is the key distinction. High LH with high testosterone would mean the feedback loop had stopped working at the pituitary end. Low LH with high testosterone is the pattern of exogenous androgen use, where the drug suppresses the axis.

cards.q: Human chorionic gonadotropin is given to an adult man. Predict the effect on his testosterone.
cards.a: Testosterone rises, because hCG acts on the LH receptor.
options: Testosterone rises, because hCG acts on the LH receptor
Testosterone falls, because hCG suppresses the pituitary
Testosterone is unchanged, because hCG acts only on ovarian tissue
Testosterone falls, because hCG competes with LH at the receptor
cards.explanation: Human chorionic gonadotropin binds the same receptor as LH and has a longer half life, so it drives Leydig cells to make more testosterone. It does not act as a pituitary suppressant, and the resulting testosterone rise is what eventually lowers LH. The LH receptor is present on Leydig cells as well as on ovarian cells, so the effect is not sex specific. hCG is an agonist rather than a competitive blocker, so it activates the receptor rather than silencing it.

cards.q: A man is treated with a 5 alpha reductase inhibitor. Which effect is expected?
cards.a: Reduced prostate growth.
options: Reduced serum testosterone
Reduced luteinizing hormone secretion
Reduced Sertoli cell inhibin output
Reduced prostate growth
cards.explanation: Prostate growth depends on dihydrotestosterone rather than on testosterone itself, so blocking the converting enzyme shrinks that stimulus. Serum testosterone does not fall and may rise slightly, because the block is downstream of testosterone synthesis. LH is governed by testosterone and estradiol feedback, which the inhibitor leaves largely intact. Inhibin comes from Sertoli cells responding to FSH, a pathway this drug does not touch.

cards.q: An aromatase inhibitor is given to a man. Predict the effect on luteinizing hormone.
cards.a: LH rises, because estradiol contributes to negative feedback.
options: LH falls, because aromatase is required for GnRH release
LH rises, because estradiol contributes to negative feedback
LH falls, because testosterone accumulates and suppresses the axis
LH is unchanged, because only estrogen feedback matters in women
cards.explanation: A surprising amount of male negative feedback at the hypothalamus is carried by estradiol made locally from testosterone, so blocking aromatase removes part of the brake and LH rises. Testosterone does accumulate, but the net effect on the axis is disinhibition rather than suppression, since the estradiol arm is gone. Estrogen feedback is not exclusive to women, and this experiment is the classic demonstration. Aromatase is not part of the machinery that releases GnRH.

cards.q: Trauma disrupts the blood testis barrier. What is the expected consequence?
cards.a: An immune response is mounted against the man's own sperm.
options: Follicle stimulating hormone secretion is permanently abolished
An immune response is mounted against the man's own sperm
Testosterone synthesis by Leydig cells stops immediately
Sperm mature faster because nutrients reach them more directly
cards.explanation: The barrier hides haploid germ cell antigens from lymphocytes, so breaching it can expose those antigens and produce antisperm antibodies. Leydig cells sit outside the barrier in the interstitium, so their testosterone output does not depend on it. Faster maturation is not what happens, because the barrier also maintains the specialized fluid the germ cells need. FSH secretion is controlled by the pituitary and inhibin feedback and would not be permanently abolished by local trauma.

cards.q: Why is testosterone from Leydig cells more effective at supporting spermatogenesis than an equal amount injected into a vein?
cards.a: Leydig cells create a very high concentration right next to the tubule.
options: Leydig cell testosterone is chemically different from the injected form
Injected testosterone is destroyed before it leaves the circulation
Only Leydig cell testosterone can bind the androgen receptor
Leydig cells create a very high concentration right next to the tubule
cards.explanation: Spermatogenesis needs an intratesticular androgen concentration many times higher than blood, and only local production plus androgen binding protein can achieve it. The molecule itself is identical whether made or injected, so chemistry is not the difference. Injected testosterone is not destroyed in the circulation, and in fact raises serum levels well. The androgen receptor does not distinguish source, so receptor selectivity is not the explanation.

cards.q: A man has a normal testosterone, a normal luteinizing hormone, a high follicle stimulating hormone, and a very low sperm count. Which compartment is failing?
cards.a: The Sertoli cells and seminiferous tubules.
options: The Sertoli cells and seminiferous tubules
The Leydig cells
The anterior pituitary gonadotropes
The hypothalamic GnRH neurons
cards.explanation: Normal testosterone with normal LH says the Leydig compartment and its feedback loop are intact, while a high FSH with low sperm points to loss of inhibin from failing Sertoli cells and tubules. Leydig failure would show low testosterone and high LH instead. Pituitary failure would lower both gonadotropins rather than raise FSH. A hypothalamic lesion would also lower gonadotropins, so a high FSH argues against it. This is the pattern that shows why inhibin is worth learning as a separate signal.

cards.q: A man whose pituitary gonadotropes were destroyed is given testosterone replacement. Predict his libido and his sperm count.
cards.a: Libido is restored but the sperm count stays very low.
options: Libido stays low but the sperm count recovers
Both stay low because testosterone cannot act without LH
Libido is restored but the sperm count stays very low
Both libido and sperm count are restored to normal
cards.explanation: Systemic testosterone is enough for libido, muscle, and secondary sexual characteristics, but it cannot recreate the intratesticular concentration that only LH driven Leydig cells produce, and it does nothing for the missing FSH signal to Sertoli cells. Full restoration would require replacing the gonadotropins themselves, which is why fertility treatment in this situation uses hCG and FSH rather than testosterone. Recovery of sperm without libido reverses which effect systemic testosterone can deliver. Testosterone acts perfectly well at its receptors without LH, so total failure is not the outcome.

cards.q: A testis remains in the abdomen instead of descending into the scrotum. Predict the effect on spermatogenesis and on testosterone production.
cards.a: Spermatogenesis is impaired while testosterone production is preserved.
options: Spermatogenesis is preserved while testosterone production fails
Both are unaffected, because the testis is perfused well in either location
Spermatogenesis is impaired while testosterone production is preserved
Both spermatogenesis and testosterone production stop completely
cards.explanation: The germ cell compartment is temperature sensitive and is damaged at core body temperature, while Leydig cells tolerate the higher temperature and continue making testosterone. Complete failure of both would predict a boy who never virilizes, which is not what is seen. The reverse pattern misassigns the temperature sensitivity, since it is the tubule rather than the interstitium that suffers. Perfusion is not the limiting factor here, temperature is, which is the whole reason the scrotum sits outside the body.

cards.q: Follow the chain from a gonadotropin releasing hormone pulse to a mature sperm. Which step would fail first if Sertoli cells could not make androgen binding protein?
cards.a: Testosterone would not stay concentrated in the tubule, so maturation falters.
options: Testosterone would not stay concentrated in the tubule, so maturation falters
Leydig cells would stop responding to LH, so testosterone synthesis would stop
The pituitary would stop releasing FSH, so Sertoli cells would lose their signal
GnRH pulses would slow, so the whole axis would shut down
cards.explanation: Androgen binding protein sits at the last link in the chain, holding testosterone in the tubular fluid where germ cells need it, so losing it breaks maturation while everything upstream still works. Leydig cells respond to LH regardless of what Sertoli cells secrete, so their synthesis continues. FSH release depends on GnRH and inhibin, not on androgen binding protein. GnRH pulse frequency is set by steroid feedback and would not change from the loss of a local carrier protein.

cards.q: Which phase of the ovarian cycle begins on day 1?
cards.a: The follicular phase.
options: The luteal phase
The ovulatory phase
The secretory phase
The follicular phase
cards.explanation: Day 1 is the first day of menstrual bleeding, and in the ovary that is the start of the follicular phase, when a cohort of follicles begins to grow under FSH. The luteal phase comes last, after ovulation, when the corpus luteum has formed. Ovulation is the brief event that separates the two, near the middle of the cycle rather than at its start. The secretory phase is a uterine phase name, and it lines up with the luteal phase of the ovary, not with day 1.

cards.q: Which ovarian phase has a nearly fixed length of about 14 days?
cards.a: The luteal phase.
options: The menstrual phase
The luteal phase
The follicular phase
The ovulatory phase
cards.explanation: The corpus luteum has a built in lifespan of roughly 14 days unless it is rescued, so the luteal phase is the constant one. The follicular phase is the variable part, which is why a 35 day cycle and a 21 day cycle differ mainly in how long it takes a dominant follicle to mature. Ovulation is a single event lasting hours rather than a two week phase. The menstrual phase is a uterine phase of about five days, not an ovarian phase of fourteen.

cards.q: Which hormone dominates the luteal phase of the ovarian cycle?
cards.a: Progesterone.
options: Luteinizing hormone
Progesterone
Estrogen
Follicle stimulating hormone
cards.explanation: The corpus luteum is primarily a progesterone factory, and progesterone is the signature hormone of the luteal phase. Estrogen dominates the follicular phase and rises again modestly in the luteal phase, but it is not the phase defining hormone. FSH is highest in the early follicular phase and is actively suppressed during the luteal phase. LH spikes at the surge and then falls back, so it is not the sustained luteal hormone.

cards.q: What does the ruptured follicle become after ovulation?
cards.a: The corpus luteum.
options: The corpus albicans
A primordial follicle
The zona pellucida
The corpus luteum
cards.explanation: The remaining granulosa and theca cells luteinize and become the corpus luteum, an endocrine structure that secretes progesterone and estrogen. The corpus albicans is the scar tissue that the corpus luteum leaves behind about two weeks later, so it is the next step rather than this one. A primordial follicle is the resting starting point of a follicle, not an end product. The zona pellucida is the glycoprotein coat around the oocyte and leaves with the egg.

cards.q: How long after the luteinizing hormone surge does ovulation typically occur?
cards.a: About 24 to 36 hours.
options: About 24 to 36 hours
About 3 to 4 hours
About 5 to 7 days
About 14 days
cards.explanation: Ovulation follows the surge by roughly a day, which is why detecting the LH rise in urine gives useful advance notice. A few hours is too fast for the follicular wall to weaken and the oocyte to complete meiosis I. Five to seven days would put ovulation in the middle of the luteal phase, after progesterone has already risen. Fourteen days is the length of the whole luteal phase, a number students often attach to the wrong interval.

cards.q: Which follicular cells produce the androgens that granulosa cells then convert to estrogen?
cards.a: Theca cells.
options: Luteal cells
Stromal cells of the medulla
Theca cells
Granulosa cells
cards.explanation: Theca cells respond to LH by making androgens, which cross to the granulosa cells where FSH driven aromatase converts them to estradiol. Granulosa cells are the converting half of that partnership and are not the androgen source. Luteal cells exist only after ovulation, so they cannot be supplying the follicular phase. Medullary stromal cells make small amounts of steroid but are not the two cell two gonadotropin partnership the follicle depends on.

cards.q: Which hormone from the growing dominant follicle helps suppress follicle stimulating hormone so the other follicles regress?
cards.a: Inhibin.
options: Progesterone
Oxytocin
Inhibin
Relaxin
cards.explanation: Inhibin from granulosa cells, together with rising estradiol, pulls FSH down, and the dominant follicle survives the drop because it has the most FSH receptors. Relaxin belongs to the luteal phase and pregnancy, loosening connective tissue rather than tuning FSH. Progesterone stays low in the follicular phase and cannot be the signal that selects the dominant follicle. Oxytocin acts on uterus and breast and has no role in follicle selection.

cards.q: If fertilization does not occur, what happens to the corpus luteum?
cards.a: It degenerates into the corpus albicans in about 14 days.
options: It degenerates into the corpus albicans in about 14 days
It persists and continues to secrete progesterone indefinitely
It converts back into a primary follicle
It is shed along with the endometrium
cards.explanation: Without hCG to rescue it, the corpus luteum has a fixed lifespan and involutes into a fibrous corpus albicans, and its falling progesterone brings on menstruation. Persistence is what happens only when a pregnancy provides hCG. A corpus luteum cannot revert to a follicle, since the follicle cell population has already been irreversibly luteinized. The corpus luteum lies in the ovary, so it is not shed with the uterine lining.

cards.q: A woman has a consistent 35 day cycle. Which phase is longer than in a 28 day cycle?
cards.a: The follicular phase.
options: The luteal phase
Both phases are proportionally longer
The ovulatory phase
The follicular phase
cards.explanation: The luteal phase is fixed near 14 days by the corpus luteum's lifespan, so all the extra time in a long cycle sits in the follicular phase while a dominant follicle takes longer to mature. Extending the luteal phase would require rescuing the corpus luteum, which happens only in pregnancy. Proportional stretching of both phases contradicts the fixed luteal length that makes cycle length prediction possible. Ovulation is an event of hours and does not stretch to fill extra days.

cards.q: A woman has a regular 35 day cycle. On approximately which day does she ovulate?
cards.a: Day 21.
options: Day 28
Day 21
Day 14
Day 17
cards.explanation: Counting back the fixed 14 day luteal phase from day 35 puts ovulation near day 21. Day 14 assumes a 28 day cycle and is the most common error, since it counts forward from day 1 rather than backward from the next menses. Day 17 would be the midpoint of the cycle, but ovulation is not anchored to the midpoint. Day 28 would leave only seven days for the corpus luteum, which is shorter than its natural lifespan.

cards.q: During the early follicular phase, estradiol is low and rising slowly. What effect does it have on luteinizing hormone?
cards.a: It suppresses LH through negative feedback.
options: It raises LH slowly in proportion to its own rise
It suppresses LH through negative feedback
It drives an LH surge through positive feedback
It has no effect until progesterone appears
cards.explanation: At low concentrations and over short exposures, estradiol exerts classic negative feedback and keeps LH modest, which is the state for most of the follicular phase. Positive feedback appears only when estradiol is both high and sustained for a day or two, which is a late follicular condition. Progesterone is not required for estradiol to have an effect, and it stays low before ovulation. A smooth proportional rise would eliminate the sharp surge that ovulation depends on.

cards.q: Progesterone rises after ovulation. What does it do to gonadotropin releasing hormone pulse frequency?
cards.a: It slows the pulses.
options: It speeds up the pulses
It stops the pulses entirely
It leaves the frequency unchanged but raises pulse height
It slows the pulses
cards.explanation: Progesterone slows the hypothalamic pulse generator, which lowers LH and favors FSH on a per pulse basis while total gonadotropin output stays down. Speeding the pulses is the late follicular pattern that helps build toward the surge, not the luteal pattern. Pulses do not stop completely, since some gonadotropin support is needed to maintain the corpus luteum. Raising pulse amplitude without changing frequency is not the described effect of luteal progesterone.

cards.q: The luteinizing hormone surge acts on the dominant follicle. Which change does it produce in the oocyte?
cards.a: The oocyte completes meiosis I and arrests in metaphase II.
options: The oocyte completes meiosis I and arrests in metaphase II
The oocyte completes meiosis II and becomes haploid
The oocyte begins meiosis I for the first time
The oocyte re-enters mitosis to produce more oocytes
cards.explanation: The oocyte has been arrested in prophase I since before birth, and the LH surge is the signal that lets it finish meiosis I and stop again at metaphase II. Meiosis II is completed only if a sperm fertilizes the egg, so it happens after ovulation rather than before. Meiosis I actually begins in fetal life, so the surge resumes it rather than starting it. Oocytes do not divide by mitosis after the fetal period, so no new oocytes are made.

cards.q: A woman has a regular 21 day cycle. Approximately how long is her luteal phase?
cards.a: About 14 days, so she ovulates near day 7.
options: About 7 days, half of the shortened cycle
About 21 days, matching her cycle length
About 14 days, so she ovulates near day 7
About 10 days, scaled down with the shorter cycle
cards.explanation: The luteal phase holds near 14 days regardless of cycle length, so a 21 day cycle means the follicular phase is compressed to about a week and ovulation occurs around day 7. Scaling the luteal phase down assumes both halves stretch and shrink together, which is the misconception this card targets. A 7 day luteal phase would be a genuinely abnormal short luteal phase, not the expected finding. A luteal phase equal to the whole cycle would leave no time for follicle growth at all.

cards.q: Which observation best confirms that ovulation has already occurred?
cards.a: A rise in serum progesterone about a week later.
options: A single high luteinizing hormone value
A fall in follicle stimulating hormone at midcycle
A rise in serum progesterone about a week later
A rise in serum estradiol in the days beforehand
cards.explanation: Progesterone only reaches high levels once a corpus luteum has formed, so a mid luteal progesterone rise is the retrospective proof that ovulation happened. Estradiol rises before ovulation and would be present even in a cycle where the surge failed. A high LH value shows a surge occurred but not that the follicle actually ruptured. A midcycle FSH fall accompanies dominant follicle selection and says nothing definitive about rupture.

cards.q: A gonadotropin releasing hormone antagonist is given on day 12 of a 28 day cycle. Predict the luteinizing hormone surge, ovulation, and the fate of the dominant follicle.
cards.a: No surge, no ovulation, and the follicle persists without rupturing.
options: No surge, no ovulation, and the follicle persists without rupturing
The surge still occurs because estradiol acts directly on the ovary
Ovulation occurs early because the follicle is released from inhibition
The follicle luteinizes immediately and progesterone rises on schedule
cards.explanation: The surge is a pituitary event that requires GnRH signaling, so blocking the receptor prevents the LH rise, and without LH the follicle neither ruptures nor luteinizes. Estradiol drives the surge by acting on the hypothalamus and pituitary, not by acting on the ovary directly, so it cannot bypass the block. Nothing about this drug releases the follicle from inhibition, so early ovulation is backwards. Luteinization also depends on LH, so progesterone cannot rise on schedule. This is exactly why these antagonists are used to prevent premature surges in assisted reproduction.

cards.q: The corpus luteum is removed on day 20 of a nonpregnant 28 day cycle. Predict progesterone and the timing of menstruation.
cards.a: Progesterone falls sharply and menstruation begins early.
options: Progesterone falls but menstruation is delayed past day 28
Progesterone is maintained by the ovary's other follicles
Progesterone falls and the next follicular phase is blocked
Progesterone falls sharply and menstruation begins early
cards.explanation: The corpus luteum is the sole significant source of progesterone in a nonpregnant cycle, so removing it drops progesterone at once, and endometrial support collapses, bringing menstruation forward. Delay would require continued progesterone, which is precisely what has been removed. Other follicles are not luteinized and cannot substitute as a progesterone source. Losing progesterone actually releases the axis, so the next follicular phase starts sooner rather than being blocked.

cards.q: An ovarian tumor secretes a constant high level of estradiol month after month. Predict follicle stimulating hormone and follicle recruitment.
cards.a: FSH is suppressed and normal follicle recruitment fails.
options: FSH surges monthly and produces repeated ovulations
FSH is suppressed and normal follicle recruitment fails
FSH is elevated and many follicles are recruited each month
FSH is normal because only inhibin controls it
cards.explanation: Constant high estradiol holds the axis under steady negative feedback, so FSH stays low and the cohort of follicles that needs an FSH rise never gets recruited. Elevated FSH would require loss of feedback rather than an excess of the feedback hormone. Inhibin is one FSH regulator but estradiol is another, so calling FSH indifferent to estradiol is wrong. Repeated ovulations would require repeated surges, and constant rather than rising estradiol does not generate the surge pattern.

cards.q: Basal body temperature is recorded daily and rises about half a degree partway through the cycle, then stays up. Explain what caused the rise and what it tells you.
cards.a: Progesterone from the corpus luteum raised the set point, so ovulation is past.
options: Falling FSH lowered heat loss, so a follicle is still maturing
Progesterone from the corpus luteum raised the set point, so ovulation is past
The estradiol peak raised the set point, so ovulation should occur in a day or two
The LH surge itself raised the set point, so ovulation is happening now
cards.explanation: Progesterone is thermogenic and shifts the hypothalamic temperature set point upward, so a sustained rise means a corpus luteum has formed and ovulation is already behind you. Estradiol does not raise the set point and in fact tends to lower it slightly, so it cannot be the source of the shift. The LH surge precedes the temperature rise by a day or more and is not itself thermogenic. FSH has no direct effect on thermoregulation. This is why temperature charting confirms ovulation retrospectively rather than predicting it.

cards.q: Which uterine phase corresponds in time to the follicular phase of the ovary?
cards.a: The proliferative phase.
options: The secretory phase
The menstrual phase
The luteal phase
The proliferative phase
cards.explanation: While follicles grow and pour out estradiol, the endometrium rebuilds itself, so the proliferative phase and the follicular phase are the same interval seen from two organs. The secretory phase lines up with the luteal phase instead, after progesterone appears. The menstrual phase is the first few days of the follicular phase, not the whole of it. Luteal is an ovarian term, not a uterine one, so it cannot be the uterine partner of anything.

cards.q: Which uterine phase corresponds in time to the luteal phase of the ovary?
cards.a: The secretory phase.
options: The secretory phase
The proliferative phase
The menstrual phase
The follicular phase
cards.explanation: Once the corpus luteum forms and progesterone rises, the endometrium switches from growing to secreting, so the secretory phase and the luteal phase occupy the same days. The proliferative phase belongs with the follicular phase and its estradiol. The menstrual phase happens after luteal progesterone withdraws, at the very start of the next cycle. Follicular is an ovarian term and cannot label a uterine phase.

cards.q: Which hormone drives the proliferative phase of the uterine cycle?
cards.a: Estrogen.
options: Luteinizing hormone
Inhibin
Estrogen
Progesterone
cards.explanation: Estradiol from growing follicles stimulates mitosis in the endometrial stroma and glands, rebuilding the lining that was just shed. Progesterone acts on an endometrium estrogen has already built and turns it secretory instead. LH acts on the ovary rather than on the endometrium, so it drives this phase only indirectly. Inhibin acts on the pituitary to lower FSH and has no direct uterine effect.

cards.q: Which hormone drives the secretory phase of the uterine cycle?
cards.a: Progesterone.
options: Follicle stimulating hormone
Human chorionic gonadotropin
Progesterone
Estrogen
cards.explanation: Progesterone from the corpus luteum converts a thickened endometrium into one with coiled glands secreting glycogen rich fluid, ready to receive an embryo. Estrogen builds the lining first but does not by itself make it secretory. FSH acts on granulosa cells in the ovary and has no endometrial receptor role here. Human chorionic gonadotropin appears only if an embryo implants, well after the secretory phase has begun.

cards.q: Which layer of the endometrium is shed during menstruation?
cards.a: The stratum functionalis.
options: The stratum functionalis
The stratum basalis
The myometrium
The perimetrium
cards.explanation: The functionalis is the superficial layer supplied by spiral arteries, and it is the layer built up and then lost each cycle. The basalis is retained and is the source of the cells that regenerate the functionalis afterward. The myometrium is the smooth muscle wall and stays in place, contracting to help expel the shed tissue. The perimetrium is the outer serous covering and is never shed.

cards.q: What immediate hormonal change triggers menstruation?
cards.a: A fall in both estrogen and progesterone.
options: A rise in both estrogen and progesterone
A rise in follicle stimulating hormone alone
A fall in luteinizing hormone alone
A fall in both estrogen and progesterone
cards.explanation: When the corpus luteum involutes, estrogen and progesterone both drop, the spiral arteries constrict, and the functionalis loses its blood supply and sloughs. A rise in these steroids maintains the lining rather than shedding it. FSH rises after menstruation begins as a consequence of the steroid withdrawal, so it follows rather than causes the event. LH has already fallen back after the surge, and its decline is not what times menstruation.

cards.q: In a standard 28 day cycle, which days make up the menstrual phase?
cards.a: Days 1 to 5.
options: Days 12 to 16
Days 1 to 5
Days 6 to 14
Days 15 to 28
cards.explanation: Menstrual flow occupies roughly the first five days, and by convention the first day of bleeding is day 1 of the cycle. Days 6 to 14 describe the proliferative phase that follows. Days 15 to 28 describe the secretory phase after ovulation. Days 12 to 16 span the periovulatory window, which sits in the middle of the cycle rather than at the beginning.

cards.q: What does progesterone do to the endometrial glands during the secretory phase?
cards.a: Makes them coil and secrete glycogen rich fluid.
options: Makes them absorb fluid from the uterine cavity
Makes them coil and secrete glycogen rich fluid
Makes them divide rapidly and thicken the lining
Makes them constrict their spiral arteries
cards.explanation: Progesterone finishes the job estrogen started, turning straight glands into tortuous ones that secrete nutrient rich fluid to support an embryo before the placenta exists. Rapid division and thickening is the estrogen driven proliferative change that comes first. Spiral artery constriction happens when progesterone is withdrawn, not while it is present. The secretory endometrium adds fluid to the cavity rather than absorbing it.

cards.q: A progesterone receptor blocker is given during the mid secretory phase. Predict the effect on the endometrium.
cards.a: The lining loses its support and begins to break down.
options: The lining continues to thicken through proliferation
The lining becomes more secretory than usual
The lining is unaffected because progesterone acts only on the ovary
The lining loses its support and begins to break down
cards.explanation: Progesterone is what holds the secretory endometrium together, so blocking its receptor mimics progesterone withdrawal and the lining sheds. Continued proliferation would need unopposed estrogen action, and the endometrium in this phase is already past that stage. Increased secretion would require more progesterone signaling, not less. Progesterone acts strongly on the endometrium, so calling its effect ovary only misplaces the target tissue.

cards.q: A woman receives estrogen for many months with no progesterone. Predict the state of her endometrium.
cards.a: It thickens continuously without becoming secretory.
options: It thickens continuously without becoming secretory
It becomes thin and atrophic
It becomes fully secretory and then sheds on schedule
It stays exactly at its baseline thickness
cards.explanation: Unopposed estrogen drives proliferation with nothing to stop it or convert it, so the lining keeps thickening and never organizes into a secretory pattern. Thinning is what a progestin alone would eventually produce, which is the opposite exposure. A secretory change requires progesterone, which by definition is absent here. Baseline thickness would mean estrogen had no proliferative effect, contradicting its central role in the proliferative phase.

cards.q: A woman has cycles in which no follicle ever ovulates. Which uterine phase never occurs?
cards.a: The secretory phase.
options: The menstrual phase
All three phases occur normally
The secretory phase
The proliferative phase
cards.explanation: No ovulation means no corpus luteum, no progesterone, and therefore no secretory transformation, even though estrogen from developing follicles still drives proliferation. The proliferative phase does occur, because follicles produce estradiol whether or not they rupture. Bleeding still occurs, though it tends to be irregular breakthrough bleeding from an overgrown lining rather than true progesterone withdrawal menses. Saying all three occur ignores that the secretory phase has a strict hormonal prerequisite.

cards.q: What effect does luteal phase progesterone have on the myometrium?
cards.a: It quiets contractile activity.
options: It has no effect on smooth muscle
It increases oxytocin receptor density
It quiets contractile activity
It increases contractile activity
cards.explanation: Progesterone keeps the uterine muscle quiet, which protects a possible implantation and later maintains pregnancy. Increased contractility is the estrogen leaning state seen at term when the progesterone to estrogen balance shifts. Progesterone acts strongly on smooth muscle throughout the body, so no effect is wrong. Raising oxytocin receptor density is an estrogen effect near term, and progesterone tends to hold that number down.

cards.q: Cervical mucus is thin, watery, and stretchy at midcycle. Which hormonal state produces this?
cards.a: High estrogen with low progesterone.
options: High estrogen with low progesterone
High progesterone with low estrogen
High progesterone with high estrogen
Low estrogen with low progesterone
cards.explanation: Peak estradiol just before ovulation thins cervical mucus so sperm can pass through it, which is the point of the change. High progesterone does the opposite, making mucus thick and hostile, which is a phase later and also part of how progestin contraceptives work. Both hormones high describes the mid luteal phase, where the progesterone effect dominates. Both low describes the menstrual phase, where mucus is scant rather than stretchy.

cards.q: What causes the ischemia that precedes shedding of the endometrium?
cards.a: Constriction of the spiral arteries.
options: Dilation of the spiral arteries
Thrombosis of the uterine vein
Loss of the stratum basalis blood supply
Constriction of the spiral arteries
cards.explanation: Withdrawal of estrogen and progesterone triggers local prostaglandin release and spiral artery constriction, and the functionalis dies from the loss of perfusion. Dilation would increase blood flow and preserve the tissue rather than destroy it. Venous thrombosis is not part of the normal cycle. The basalis keeps its own straight arterial supply, which is exactly why it survives to regenerate the lining.

cards.q: An endometrial thickness measured on day 12 is much greater than one measured on day 3 of the same cycle. What explains the difference?
cards.a: Estrogen from growing follicles has driven proliferation.
options: Falling FSH has allowed the lining to rebuild
Estrogen from growing follicles has driven proliferation
Progesterone from the corpus luteum has driven secretion
The LH surge has thickened the lining directly
cards.explanation: Day 3 is just after shedding, when only the basalis remains, and by day 12 estradiol has rebuilt a thick functionalis. Progesterone cannot be the explanation, because no corpus luteum exists before ovulation. The LH surge has not yet happened on day 12, and in any case it acts on the follicle rather than on the endometrium. FSH acts on granulosa cells, so its fall does not directly rebuild the lining.

cards.q: An endometrial sample taken on day 22 shows tortuous glands full of glycogen rich secretion. What does that tell you about the ovary?
cards.a: A functioning corpus luteum is present and secreting progesterone.
options: An LH surge is about to occur within the next day
A functioning corpus luteum is present and secreting progesterone
A dominant follicle is still growing and secreting estradiol
The ovary has failed and produces neither steroid
cards.explanation: A secretory endometrium is direct evidence of progesterone action, and in a nonpregnant cycle the only meaningful progesterone source is a corpus luteum, so ovulation must have occurred. A growing follicle produces estradiol, which gives a proliferative rather than secretory picture. Ovarian failure would leave a thin inactive lining. An imminent surge belongs to the late follicular phase, when the endometrium is still proliferative.

cards.q: A woman's progesterone remains elevated past the expected day of menstruation and she does not bleed. What is the most likely sequence of events?
cards.a: An embryo implanted and hCG rescued the corpus luteum, so progesterone continued.
options: The corpus luteum involuted early and the endometrium became atrophic
Estrogen rose sharply and converted the secretory endometrium back to proliferative
FSH rose and recruited a new follicle that secreted the progesterone
An embryo implanted and hCG rescued the corpus luteum, so progesterone continued
cards.explanation: Human chorionic gonadotropin from the implanting embryo binds the LH receptor on the corpus luteum, keeping it alive past its normal 14 day lifespan, so progesterone never withdraws and menstruation never starts. Early involution would drop progesterone and bring bleeding forward, the opposite of what is described. Estrogen cannot reverse a secretory endometrium back into a proliferative one. New follicles make estradiol rather than progesterone, so recruitment does not explain the sustained level.

cards.q: A woman ovulates normally but her luteal progesterone rises only to about half the usual level. Predict the endometrium and the length of her luteal phase.
cards.a: Incomplete secretory development and a shortened luteal phase.
options: Incomplete secretory development and a shortened luteal phase
Full secretory development and a normal 14 day luteal phase
Continued proliferation and a lengthened luteal phase
An atrophic lining with no bleeding at all
cards.explanation: Secretory transformation is dose dependent, so weak progesterone gives an endometrium that is out of step with the calendar, and the underperforming corpus luteum also involutes sooner, shortening the phase. Full development at half the hormone would mean the endometrial response has no dose dependence. Continued proliferation would require the absence of progesterone rather than a reduced amount, and less progesterone shortens rather than lengthens the phase. An atrophic non bleeding lining is what long term progestin exposure produces, which is a different situation.

cards.q: Follow the cycle in order: estradiol climbs from day 6 to day 13, an LH surge occurs, then progesterone rises from day 16 onward. Match the uterine phases to those events.
cards.a: Proliferative through day 14, then secretory from about day 15 to 28.
options: Proliferative for the whole cycle, since estrogen is present throughout
Menstrual through day 14, then proliferative from about day 15 to 28
Proliferative through day 14, then secretory from about day 15 to 28
Secretory through day 14, then proliferative from about day 15 to 28
cards.explanation: Estradiol builds the lining during the follicular phase, so those days are proliferative, and the progesterone that follows ovulation converts it to secretory for the second half. Reversing the two ignores that secretion requires progesterone, which is not present before ovulation. Calling the whole cycle proliferative overlooks the progesterone driven change even though estrogen is indeed present in both halves. Menstruation occupies only the first five days, not the first two weeks.

cards.q: Which tissue secretes human chorionic gonadotropin in early pregnancy?
cards.a: The syncytiotrophoblast of the embryo.
options: The anterior pituitary of the mother
The endometrial glands of the uterine lining
The syncytiotrophoblast of the embryo
The corpus luteum of the ovary
cards.explanation: The outer trophoblast layer of the implanting embryo makes hCG, which is why the hormone appears only after implantation and why it signals that an embryo is present. The corpus luteum is the target of hCG rather than its source. The maternal anterior pituitary makes LH and FSH, and its output actually falls during pregnancy. Endometrial glands secrete nutrient fluid but not gonadotropins.

cards.q: Which receptor does human chorionic gonadotropin act on?
cards.a: The luteinizing hormone receptor.
options: The luteinizing hormone receptor
The follicle stimulating hormone receptor
The progesterone receptor
The oxytocin receptor
cards.explanation: Human chorionic gonadotropin is structurally close enough to LH to bind and activate the LH receptor, which is exactly how it keeps the corpus luteum alive. The FSH receptor is a different glycoprotein hormone receptor and is not the target. Progesterone receptors are intracellular steroid receptors, and hCG is a peptide that cannot use them. The oxytocin receptor belongs to a separate family on uterine and breast tissue.

cards.q: What does human chorionic gonadotropin do to the corpus luteum?
cards.a: Maintains it so it keeps secreting progesterone.
options: Causes it to involute into a corpus albicans
Converts it back into a mature follicle
Stops its progesterone output but preserves its estrogen output
Maintains it so it keeps secreting progesterone
cards.explanation: By occupying the LH receptor, hCG rescues the corpus luteum from its scheduled death and keeps progesterone flowing so the endometrium is not shed. Involution is exactly what hCG prevents, and it is what happens in a nonpregnant cycle. A corpus luteum cannot revert to a follicle, since luteinization is irreversible. Progesterone output is the main thing hCG sustains, so selectively stopping it reverses the hormone's purpose.

cards.q: Around which week of pregnancy does the placenta take over progesterone production from the corpus luteum?
cards.a: Around weeks 7 to 10.
options: Only in the final two weeks
Around weeks 7 to 10
Around weeks 2 to 3
Around weeks 20 to 24
cards.explanation: The luteal placental shift happens near the end of the first trimester, which is why the corpus luteum is essential early and dispensable later. Weeks 2 to 3 is far too early, since the placenta is barely formed and hCG is only just rising. Weeks 20 to 24 is well past the point where removing the corpus luteum is safe. Waiting until the final two weeks would leave most of pregnancy dependent on a structure that cannot last that long.

cards.q: Which hormone do home pregnancy tests detect?
cards.a: Human chorionic gonadotropin.
options: Human placental lactogen
Human chorionic gonadotropin
Progesterone
Estriol
cards.explanation: Human chorionic gonadotropin is detectable in urine within days of implantation and is unique to pregnancy, which makes it the ideal test target. Progesterone is high in every luteal phase, pregnant or not, so it cannot distinguish the two. Estriol rises later in pregnancy and is not sensitive in the first weeks. Human placental lactogen also appears too late and in a pattern less specific than hCG.

cards.q: What is the main action of relaxin during pregnancy?
cards.a: It softens the pubic ligaments, symphysis, and cervix.
options: It maintains the corpus luteum after implantation
It stimulates milk synthesis in the mammary gland
It raises maternal blood glucose to feed the growing fetus
It softens the pubic ligaments, symphysis, and cervix
cards.explanation: Relaxin, from the corpus luteum and later the placenta, loosens pelvic connective tissue and helps ripen the cervix in preparation for delivery. Maintaining the corpus luteum is the job of hCG. Milk synthesis is driven by prolactin once the steroid block is lifted at delivery. Raising maternal glucose is largely a human placental lactogen effect, which creates insulin resistance to spare glucose for the fetus.

cards.q: Which hormone is chiefly responsible for keeping the uterus quiet during pregnancy?
cards.a: Progesterone.
options: Progesterone
Estrogen
Oxytocin
Prostaglandin F2 alpha
cards.explanation: Progesterone suppresses myometrial excitability and holds down oxytocin receptor expression, keeping the uterus from contracting until term. Estrogen does the opposite, increasing contractility and oxytocin receptor density as term approaches. Oxytocin is the hormone that drives contractions once the uterus becomes responsive. Prostaglandins also promote contractions and cervical ripening rather than quiescence.

cards.q: Placental estrogen synthesis depends on a precursor supplied by which structure?
cards.a: The fetal adrenal cortex.
options: The fetal liver alone
The maternal thyroid gland
The fetal adrenal cortex
The maternal ovary
cards.explanation: The placenta lacks a key enzyme and cannot build the steroid backbone from scratch, so it relies on androgen precursor from the fetal adrenal cortex, making the two organs a single functional unit. The maternal ovary contributes little once the placenta has taken over. The fetal liver does participate by hydroxylating the precursor but is not the origin of it. The thyroid makes iodinated amine hormones and has no role in steroid supply.

cards.q: The corpus luteum is removed at week 6 of pregnancy without hormone replacement. Predict the outcome.
cards.a: Progesterone falls and the pregnancy is lost.
options: Progesterone falls but hCG rises enough to maintain the endometrium
Progesterone rises because the ovary no longer suppresses the placenta
Progesterone falls and the pregnancy is lost
Progesterone is maintained by the placenta and the pregnancy continues
cards.explanation: At week 6 the placenta cannot yet supply enough progesterone, so removing the corpus luteum drops progesterone and the endometrium cannot be maintained. Placental rescue is what happens after the luteal placental shift near weeks 7 to 10, not before it. Human chorionic gonadotropin works by driving the corpus luteum, so with that structure gone hCG has no target and cannot substitute. The ovary does not suppress the placenta, so removing it cannot raise progesterone.

cards.q: The corpus luteum is removed at week 12 of pregnancy. Predict the outcome.
cards.a: The pregnancy continues because the placenta now makes progesterone.
options: The pregnancy continues because the placenta now makes progesterone
The pregnancy is lost because progesterone falls sharply
The pregnancy continues only if hCG is given
The pregnancy continues but relaxin excess causes early labor
cards.explanation: By week 12 the luteal placental shift is complete, so the placenta supplies enough progesterone and the corpus luteum is no longer required. Loss of the pregnancy is the week 6 answer, and the difference between the two timings is the point of this pair. Giving hCG would not help, since there is no corpus luteum left for it to act on. Removing the corpus luteum reduces rather than increases relaxin, so relaxin excess does not follow.

cards.q: Human chorionic gonadotropin peaks near week 10 and then declines. Why does progesterone not fall along with it?
cards.a: The placenta has taken over progesterone synthesis by then.
options: The corpus luteum becomes independent of any hormonal support
The maternal pituitary begins secreting LH to replace hCG
Progesterone has a half life long enough to last the pregnancy
The placenta has taken over progesterone synthesis by then
cards.explanation: The hCG decline is safe precisely because the placenta is now the dominant progesterone source and needs no gonadotropin to keep producing. A corpus luteum does not become self sustaining, and it involutes as hCG falls. Maternal LH is suppressed during pregnancy by high steroid levels, so the pituitary does not step in. Steroid half lives are measured in minutes to hours, so stored hormone cannot carry a pregnancy for months.

cards.q: Progesterone is elevated throughout pregnancy. Predict its effect on maternal ventilation and arterial PCO2.
cards.a: Ventilation increases and PCO2 falls.
options: Ventilation is unchanged and PCO2 falls
Ventilation increases and PCO2 falls
Ventilation decreases and PCO2 rises
Ventilation increases and PCO2 rises
cards.explanation: Progesterone stimulates the respiratory center, so pregnant women hyperventilate mildly and arterial PCO2 settles around 30 mmHg, which also helps carbon dioxide move from fetus to mother. Reduced ventilation with a higher PCO2 would work against fetal gas exchange and is the opposite of the measured pattern. Ventilation up with PCO2 up is internally inconsistent, since more ventilation blows off carbon dioxide. Ventilation must change for PCO2 to fall, so unchanged ventilation with a low PCO2 does not follow.

cards.q: The alpha subunit of human chorionic gonadotropin is nearly identical to that of thyroid stimulating hormone. Predict the thyroid effect of very high hCG in early pregnancy.
cards.a: Mild thyroid stimulation with a slightly suppressed TSH.
options: Complete loss of thyroid hormone production
Mild thyroid stimulation with a slightly suppressed TSH
Mild thyroid suppression with a raised TSH
No thyroid effect, because the beta subunits differ
cards.explanation: At high concentrations hCG weakly cross activates the TSH receptor, nudging thyroid hormone up, and the resulting feedback lowers TSH slightly. Suppression with a raised TSH is the reverse of what a receptor agonist produces. The beta subunits do differ, which is why the effect is weak rather than strong, but weak is not zero when hCG is this abundant. Complete loss of production would require destruction of the gland, not weak stimulation of it.

cards.q: Which effect of progesterone explains the heartburn and constipation common in pregnancy?
cards.a: Relaxation of gastrointestinal smooth muscle.
options: Increased gastric acid secretion by the stomach
Increased intestinal motility
Reduced blood flow to the wall of the gut
Relaxation of gastrointestinal smooth muscle
cards.explanation: Progesterone relaxes smooth muscle throughout the body, so the lower esophageal sphincter loosens and intestinal transit slows. Acid secretion does not rise in pregnancy, so the reflux comes from a weak sphincter rather than more acid. Increased motility would speed transit and relieve constipation rather than cause it. Gut blood flow is not reduced in pregnancy, and blood volume actually rises substantially.

cards.q: A woman conceives through in vitro fertilization after both ovaries were removed. She receives progesterone supplementation, which is stopped at week 12. Predict the outcome and explain it.
cards.a: The pregnancy continues, because placental progesterone has replaced the missing corpus luteum.
options: The pregnancy continues, because placental progesterone has replaced the missing corpus luteum
The pregnancy is lost, because without an ovary there is no progesterone source at all
The pregnancy continues only because hCG substitutes for progesterone
The pregnancy is lost, because progesterone supplementation suppressed the placenta
cards.explanation: Supplementation is needed only to cover the window before the luteal placental shift, and by week 12 the placenta produces enough progesterone on its own, so stopping then is safe. The ovary is not the only possible source, and that is precisely what the placenta demonstrates. Human chorionic gonadotropin is a gonadotropin, not a steroid, so it cannot substitute for progesterone in maintaining the endometrium. Exogenous progesterone does not suppress placental steroid output.

cards.q: A fetus has a severely underdeveloped adrenal cortex. Predict maternal estriol and explain why.
cards.a: Maternal estriol is low, because the placenta lacks its androgen precursor.
options: Maternal estriol is normal, because it comes from the maternal ovary
Maternal estriol is low, because the fetal adrenal normally destroys estrogen
Maternal estriol is low, because the placenta lacks its androgen precursor
Maternal estriol is high, because the placenta compensates by making more
cards.explanation: The placenta cannot make the steroid backbone itself, so it depends on androgen precursor from the fetal adrenal cortex, and losing that supply drops maternal estriol. The placenta cannot compensate, because the missing step is an enzyme it does not possess. The maternal ovary is largely quiescent during pregnancy and is not the estriol source. The fetal adrenal supplies precursor rather than destroying estrogen, so the direction of that reasoning is backwards.

cards.q: Trace the events after implantation. Which sequence correctly links human chorionic gonadotropin to the survival of the pregnancy?
cards.a: Trophoblast secretes hCG, hCG binds LH receptors on the corpus luteum, progesterone stays high, the endometrium is maintained.
options: The corpus luteum secretes hCG, the trophoblast responds, estrogen rises, the endometrium is maintained
The maternal pituitary secretes hCG, the corpus luteum responds, relaxin rises, the endometrium is maintained
Trophoblast secretes hCG, hCG binds LH receptors on the corpus luteum, progesterone stays high, the endometrium is maintained
Trophoblast secretes hCG, hCG acts on the endometrium directly, progesterone is not needed, menstruation is prevented
cards.explanation: The chain runs from embryo to ovary to uterus: the trophoblast makes hCG, hCG keeps the corpus luteum alive through the LH receptor, and the progesterone that results holds the secretory endometrium in place. Human chorionic gonadotropin has no direct endometrial action that could replace progesterone. The corpus luteum is the responder rather than the source, so reversing those two breaks the logic. The maternal pituitary does not make hCG, and relaxin is not what maintains the lining.

cards.q: A pregnancy produces extremely high human chorionic gonadotropin, several times the usual peak. Which combination of findings would you expect?
cards.a: Thyroid hormone slightly elevated, TSH slightly low, and a strongly maintained corpus luteum.
options: Thyroid hormone slightly elevated, TSH slightly low, and a strongly maintained corpus luteum
Thyroid hormone slightly low, TSH slightly high, and an involuting corpus luteum
Thyroid hormone unchanged, TSH unchanged, and an involuting corpus luteum
Thyroid hormone strongly elevated, TSH strongly elevated, and a maintained corpus luteum
cards.explanation: Very high hCG both drives the LH receptor hard, keeping the corpus luteum robust, and weakly cross activates the TSH receptor, raising thyroid hormone enough to feed back and lower TSH. The opposite thyroid pattern would mean hCG blocked rather than stimulated the receptor. Unchanged thyroid values ignore how much cross reactivity matters at these concentrations. Thyroid hormone and TSH cannot both be strongly elevated when the feedback loop is intact, because rising thyroid hormone suppresses TSH.

cards.q: Where is oxytocin synthesized and from where is it released?
cards.a: Made in the hypothalamus, released by the posterior pituitary.
options: Made and released entirely by the anterior pituitary
Made in the uterine wall, released into uterine veins
Made in the placenta, released into the maternal circulation
Made in the hypothalamus, released by the posterior pituitary
cards.explanation: Hypothalamic neurons make oxytocin and send it down their axons to nerve terminals in the posterior pituitary, where it enters the blood. The anterior pituitary makes its own hormones from glandular cells and does not store oxytocin. The uterus is a target of oxytocin, carrying receptors for it, rather than a source. The placenta makes many hormones but is not the origin of the oxytocin that drives labor.

cards.q: Which hormone drives milk synthesis in the mammary gland?
cards.a: Prolactin.
options: Relaxin
Prolactin
Oxytocin
Estrogen
cards.explanation: Prolactin from the anterior pituitary stimulates the alveolar cells to make milk, which is the production half of lactation. Oxytocin handles the other half, ejecting milk that has already been made. Estrogen helps the ducts develop during pregnancy but blocks actual milk production until it falls at delivery. Relaxin loosens pelvic connective tissue and has no lactogenic role.

cards.q: Which hormone causes milk ejection, sometimes called let down?
cards.a: Oxytocin.
options: Human placental lactogen
Oxytocin
Prolactin
Progesterone
cards.explanation: Oxytocin contracts the myoepithelial cells wrapped around the alveoli, squeezing milk into the ducts so the infant can obtain it. Prolactin makes the milk but cannot move it, which is why the two hormones are learned as a pair. Progesterone actually blocks milk production during pregnancy and has no ejection role. Human placental lactogen prepares the breast during pregnancy but does not trigger let down.

cards.q: Which cells contract to eject milk from the alveoli?
cards.a: Myoepithelial cells.
options: Alveolar secretory cells
Ductal epithelial cells
Smooth muscle cells of the nipple
Myoepithelial cells
cards.explanation: Myoepithelial cells form a contractile basket around each alveolus and squeeze when oxytocin binds. Alveolar secretory cells make the milk but do not contract. Ductal epithelium lines the passageways and conducts milk rather than propelling it. There is no meaningful smooth muscle layer in the nipple that performs ejection.

cards.q: What holds prolactin secretion down when a woman is not lactating?
cards.a: Tonic dopamine inhibition from the hypothalamus.
options: Tonic dopamine inhibition from the hypothalamus
Tonic somatostatin inhibition from the hypothalamus
